title: Stanford's AI Index found a 42% error rate in AI benchmarks — here's what a measurement body does about it
description: The Stanford AI Index's finding that AI benchmarks carry a 42% error rate is the industry's quiet admission: evaluation is unregulated evidence. Council of AI publishes reproducible signed measurements instead.
canon: Measurement, not certification. Not a notified body.
body: What happened. The Stanford AI Index report highlighted that error rates in AI evaluation benchmarks can reach 42% — a figure that undercuts the way the industry quotes benchmark wins. Critics who read all 414 pages pressed further: the summary itself can mislead, which is exactly the disease: evaluation evidence is narrated, not verified.

Why it matters to anyone buying AI. If a benchmark says a model is 22% safer but the harness that produced it was a different version, a different prompt set, or a different grader, the number is a story — not evidence. Procurement officers, insurers, and regulators now face the same question: 'who verified the verifier?'

What a measurement body does differently. Council of AI publishes measurement credentials rather than marketing claims: deterministic predicates with frozen gold answers, held-out item banks (kept secret so models cannot memorise them), Ed25519-signed results, RFC 9943 (SCITT) transparency receipts, and a public verify page where anyone can recompute the card client-side in 60 seconds. If a number changes, the change is a signed correction with its predecessor chained — never a silent edit.

The honest gap. A 42% error rate is not something to hide; it is the reason to demand evidence trails. Where we have not measured an axis, we say UNMEASURED — publicly — rather than inventing a number. Our published methodology paper describes exactly how our scoring works, in public, for peer review.
What you can do. When you see a benchmark claim, ask for the harness hash, the prompt set digest, the signer, and the receipt. Most claims cannot answer. Ours can.
